newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin improves, but uncertainty envelopes Russia.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin improves, but uncertainty envelopes Russia.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin is showing signs of improvement in his battle against pneumonia, but questions over when he will be able to resume his official duties are keeping Russians on tenterhooks.

The president's latest bout of ill health -- just two months after multiple heart bypass surgery -- has opened up a debate on whether Russia should alter its consitution to shift power from the president to the legislature.
At least one Moscow daily newspaper suggested it might be time for Yeltsin, 65, post-Soviet Russia's first president, to step down.
A Kremlin bulletin on Yeltsin's health issued on Saturday said doctors had noted that he was responding to treatment since entering hospital on Wednesday.
"In their opinion, the patient's condition has stabilised, his activity has grown somewhat," it said. Yeltsin's temperature was normal and his blood pressure stable.
The next bulletin was due on Sunday.

The chief Kremlin doctor told Russian public television Yeltsin had pneumonia "of medium gravity" in both lungs. He predicted the president would resume activities after a convalescence which "ideally" would continue until January 25 to 27.
"I'm sure there will be no 50-50 situation -- the president spending half the time in the Kremlin and half in hospital," Sergei Mironov told an interviewer, apparently on Friday.

"This is simply an episode, though a worrying one. Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) is the sort of person who is always saying 'Let's go, it's time to get going'. That was always the basis of his life's activity and work."

Mironov had earlier said Yeltsin needed to remain in the hospital at least until the beginning of next week. The president, he said, was a reluctant and frustrated patient who had disregarded advice to enter hospital earlier for treatment.
Yeltsin's press office issued a statement apparently showing him still dealing with state business, his signature attached to a message of thanks to a retired regional leader.
But the liberal daily Komsomolskaya Pravda suggested the time had come for Yeltsin to consider stepping aside.
"Regretfully, it is obvious that the president has no strength left to attend to affairs of state properly," it said.
Other newspapers have expressed doubts over Yeltsin's future capabilities in tackling festering problems -- arrears in paying salaries and pensions and reform of the armed forces.
Should he resign, the duties of president pass for three months to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, currently on holiday near Moscow. An election must then follow.
Yeltsin's most vocal rival, his former security chief Alexander Lebed, has called for him to quit. Politicians more sympathetic to the president have maintained a more discreet silence.
The chairman of parliament's upper house said on Friday it was time to consider amending the 1993 constitution, drawn up after Yeltsin used tanks to put down a rebellion by parliament.

A commentator on Russian public television suggested Yeltsin might also want to water down his considerable powers to guard against an authoritarian successor coming to power. But a top presidential aide warned against hasty change.

"Amending the constitution in 1992 and 1993 turned into a political battle, created competing centres of power and led to tragic events," Sergei Shakhrai told the television, referring to the October 1993 storming of parliament.
"In short, I am for discussion, but against amendments."
